title: Chapter 2 — Of Individualism In Democratic Countries
paragraphs: I have shown how, in ages of equality, every person looks for his opinions within himself. I am now going to show how, in those same ages, all his feelings turn toward himself alone. Individualism*a is a new expression, born from a new idea. Our forefathers knew only selfishness. Selfishness is a passionate and exaggerated love of self that leads a man to connect everything to his own person and to prefer himself to everything else in the world. Individualism is a mature and calm feeling that disposes each member of the community to cut himself off from the mass of his fellow creatures and to withdraw with his family and friends. Having formed this little circle of his own, he willingly leaves society at large to take care of itself. Selfishness comes from blind instinct. Individualism springs from mistaken judgment more than from corrupt feelings; it arises as much from deficiencies of the mind as from the perversity of the heart. Selfishness blights the seed of every virtue. Individualism at first only undermines the virtues of public life, but in the long run it attacks and destroys all the others, and is finally absorbed into outright selfishness. Selfishness is a vice as old as the world and belongs to no one form of society more than another. Individualism is of democratic origin, and it threatens to spread in the same proportion as equality of conditions.

[Footnote a: [I retain the expression used in the original, however strange it may sound to English ears, partly because it illustrates the remark made in an earlier chapter about the introduction of general terms into democratic language, and partly because I know of no English word that exactly corresponds to it. The chapter itself defines the meaning the author gives it. — Translator's Note.]]

Among aristocratic nations, since families remain for centuries in the same condition and often on the same piece of ground, all generations become, as it were, contemporaries. A man almost always knows his ancestors and respects them. He feels he can already see his remote descendants, and he loves them. He willingly takes on duties toward both, and he will often sacrifice his own pleasures for those who came before him and those who will come after him. Aristocratic institutions also have the effect of binding each man closely to several of his fellow citizens. Because the classes of an aristocratic people are sharply marked and permanent, each class is regarded by its own members as a kind of lesser country, more tangible and more cherished than the country at large. Since in aristocratic communities all citizens occupy fixed positions, one above the other, each of them always sees a man above him whose patronage he needs, and another below him whose cooperation he can claim. Men living in aristocratic ages are therefore almost always closely attached to something outside their own sphere, and they are often ready to forget themselves. It is true that in such ages the idea of human fellowship is faint, and men seldom think of sacrificing themselves for humanity as a whole; but they often sacrifice themselves for particular other men. In democratic ages, by contrast, when each person's duties toward the human race are much more clearly understood, devoted service to any single individual becomes rarer. The bond of human affection is stretched wider, but it is also loosened.

Among democratic nations new families are constantly springing up, others are constantly falling away, and all those that remain are changing their condition. The fabric of time is broken every instant, and the track of the generations is erased. Those who went before are soon forgotten; of those who will come after, no one has any idea. A man's interest is confined to those in close proximity to himself. As each class draws nearer to the others and blends with them, its members become indifferent and as strangers to one another. Aristocracy had made a chain of all the members of the community, from the peasant to the king. Democracy breaks that chain and severs every link. As social conditions become more equal, the number increases of those who, though neither rich enough nor powerful enough to exert great influence over their fellow creatures, have still acquired or kept enough education and property to meet their own needs. They owe nothing to anyone and expect nothing from anyone. They form the habit of always thinking of themselves as standing alone, and are apt to imagine that their whole destiny lies in their own hands. Thus democracy not only makes every man forget his ancestors; it hides his descendants from him and separates him from his contemporaries. It throws him back forever upon himself alone, and threatens in the end to confine him entirely within the solitude of his own heart.
